title: December 30, 2024 is in ISO week 1 of 2025, not week 52 of 2024
assumption: The 'year' a date belongs to for week-numbering purposes is just its calendar year.

input.display: date(2024, 12, 30).isocalendar() == (2025, 1, 1)  -- ISO week-year 2025, week 1, weekday Monday
input.description: Any report, invoice numbering, or analytics bucketing that labels data by 'year-week' (e.g. '2024-W52') using the calendar year instead of the ISO week-year.

what_goes_wrong: A 'weekly report for year X, week Y' system that pairs the calendar year with the ISO week number produces a nonsensical or wrong label like '2024-W01' for a date that is actually in the first ISO week of 2025, or silently double-counts/skips a week at the year boundary.
why: ISO 8601 defines week 1 of a year as the week containing that year's first Thursday (equivalently, the week containing January 4th), and weeks run Monday-Sunday. Because of this rule, the last few days of December can fall into week 1 of the FOLLOWING year (as with 2024-12-30, a Monday, which starts the week containing 2025-01-02, a Thursday), and conversely the first few days of January can belong to the last week of the PREVIOUS year. The ISO week-year (`%G` in strftime, `isocalendar()[0]` in Python) is therefore a distinct value from the plain calendar year (`%Y`), and the two disagree exactly in this boundary zone.

repros.code:
from datetime import date

d = date(2024, 12, 30)
print("calendar year:", d.year)
print("isocalendar:", d.isocalendar())
print(d.strftime("%G-W%V"), "vs plain %Y:", d.strftime("%Y"))
repros.expected_output:
calendar year: 2024
isocalendar: datetime.IsoCalendarDate(year=2025, week=1, weekday=1)
2025-W01 vs plain %Y: 2024

fix: Always use the ISO week-year (`%G`), never the plain calendar year (`%Y`), when labeling data with an ISO week number (`%V`); most date libraries expose both separately specifically because they can diverge.

sources.title: ISO 8601 week date (Wikipedia overview, verify against ISO 8601:2004)
